Chapter Two: Letting Go of Excuses—Moving Beyond Self-Imposed Limitations.
Now that those hidden barriers of guilt and shame are out in the open, it’s time for the next big step: tackling the excuses that hold us back.
Excuses can feel so reassuring, can’t they? They give us an easy way out—a reason to believe change just isn’t possible right now. But here’s the thing: they also keep our biggest dreams at arm’s length.
Excuses show up in all sorts of ways. Sometimes, they’re rooted in fear—like telling yourself, “I’m not qualified,” or, “I just don’t have enough time,” or maybe, “If I try, I’ll probably fail.” Other times, they wear a mask of practicality: “It’s not the right season,” “My family needs me,” or even, “I’m too old to start over.” These stories might sound convincing, but more often than not, they’re just ways we try to dodge discomfort or risk.
Imagine your excuses as the walls of a cozy, familiar room. Sure, those walls feel safe—but they also keep your world small. Stepping outside takes courage, and it means being willing to sit with a little uncertainty.
So, how do we actually let go of excuses? It starts with a little honesty and self-reflection.
Here’s a practical way to do it: take each excuse and ask yourself, “Is this really a fact, or is it just a belief?” For example, when you think, “I don’t have time,” is it absolutely true? Or does it really reflect your priorities—or maybe even a hesitation to set boundaries? The same goes for “I’m not qualified.” Is that really about ability, or is it just a way to avoid the feeling of being new at something?
If you want to break through those excuses, try these steps:
First, pay attention to which excuses pop up again and again, and in what situations.
Next, challenge them—are they based on real evidence, or just a fear of stepping out of your comfort zone?
And finally, try changing the way you talk to yourself. Instead of saying, “I can’t,” what if you said, “I choose not to right now,” or, “I’m learning how”?
Picture this: imagine a woman who dreams of starting her own business. She keeps telling herself she doesn’t have the right skills. But when she looks closer, she realizes that, sure, she doesn’t know everything—but she’s absolutely capable of learning. The real obstacle isn’t her ability; it’s the fear of being seen as inexperienced.
Letting go of excuses isn’t about pretending real challenges don’t exist. It’s about telling the difference between genuine obstacles and the limitations we create for ourselves. And that difference matters, because it shifts your focus from what can’t be changed to what actually can.
This isn’t a one-time thing, either. Excuses will pop up again—especially when you’re facing something new or challenging. The key is to see them as signals—little reminders to pause, reflect, and choose action instead of avoidance.
And as you practice this, you’ll notice something powerful: your resilience grows, and your sense of agency gets stronger with every step.
